title: I Took the HAM-Radio Board Hours to the Operator Who Never Signed Off

parts.text: I opened the log at 8:03 p.m. and operator Vela was still on my unpaid-looking leftover net. The board said: SIGN ON. SIGN OFF. NINETY MINUTES. I was forty-nine, licensed, holding a calendar hold. Vela did not stop. "Operators are the net." I photographed the board, the hold, and her call still live. Then I logged an overlap. At 8:10 the club trustee pinged why Vela's name was on my hours. I did not argue the joke. I argued the file. A paper policy is only paper until someone treats it like a clock.
parts.cliffhanger_hint: The club trustee can see Vela's live call on the board during my HAM hours.

social.video_title: The operator never signed off my booked net — Part 1/2
social.description: HAM club, a ninety-minute board, a live leftover call. I logged the overlap. Would you have asked the trustee?

parts.text: Vela called it a net until the trustee asked for the still. I printed the overlap, the board, and the hold. She signed off. Vela booked her own ninety and told operators nets were always about optics. Optics is a word operators use when logs exist. Hours now have a second line: OPERATORS SIGN OFF. I keep my ninety. Vela schedules. The shack finally sounds like a hold, not leftover air. The rule looks ordinary now, which is the whole point.

social.description: Overlap log, a real sign-off, and a second line. Was a net ever my hold?
